ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The coccyx is the terminal vertebral segment of the spine, forming the tailbone. It provides attachment for pelvic floor muscles and supports sitting posture. Clinically, it can be a source of pain, infection, or injury, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: The coccyx is the smallest, most distal part of the vertebral column, usually consisting of 3–5 fused vertebrae. It serves as an attachment for pelvic floor and gluteal muscles and helps maintain posture when sitting.

Posteriorly, it lies below the sacrum, anterior to the gluteal muscles. Each segment has a characteristic shape: the first is wedge‑shaped, the second is triangular, the third is round, and the fourth is flat.
Anteriorly, the coccyx is adjacent to the rectum and anal canal. Posteriorly, it lies near the sacral hiatus and the coccygeal nerve roots. It is surrounded by the levator ani and coccygeus muscles.
Arterial supply comes from the coccygeal artery, a branch of the internal iliac. Venous drainage follows the same route.
The coccygeal plexus, formed by the terminal branches of S4–S5, supplies sensation to the perianal area and motor fibers to the coccygeal muscles.
Provides attachment for pelvic floor and gluteal muscles, aiding in posture and sitting. It also serves as a lever for the coccygeal muscles during certain movements.
Common issues include coccygodynia (tailbone pain), traumatic fractures, and coccygeal abscesses. In low‑resource settings, infections may arise from poor wound care or contaminated instruments.

Detects abscess; normal if no fluid collection
Pain on pressure indicates coccygodynia; swelling suggests infection

sections.p: Ask patients about pain when sitting or standing. A positive 'pinch test' indicates coccygodynia. In trauma, look for step deformity or tenderness over the coccyx.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain after trauma, fever with perianal swelling, inability to sit or stand, or signs of systemic infection

faq.a: Trauma, prolonged sitting, childbirth, or repetitive strain can irritate the coccyx and surrounding tissues.

faq.q: Can a coccyx fracture heal on its own?
faq.a: Yes, minor fractures often heal with rest, cushions, and pain relief; severe fractures may need surgical realignment.
Rare but can occur after trauma or infection; requires drainage and antibiotics.
